items.prompt:
Read the conversation:
Ella: 'I think we should plant sunflowers in our class garden.'
Jay: 'I like sunflowers too! They grow really tall — my dad grew some last year.'
Ella: 'Did they need a lot of sun?'
Jay: 'Yes, they need lots of sun and water.'

List TWO things Jay does well in this conversation.
items.answer: 1. Jay builds on Ella's idea by agreeing and adding a personal experience. 2. Jay answers Ella's question fully, staying on topic.

steps: Jay agrees and adds information from personal experience — building on Ella's idea.
Jay answers Ella's follow-up question completely and stays on the topic of sunflowers.
Jay does not interrupt or go off-topic.

items.prompt:
A student interrupts her partner mid-sentence. The partner says, 'Please let me finish.' The first student waits, listens, and then shares her idea. What did the first student do WELL at the end?
A) She talked over her partner the whole time.
B) She waited for her partner to finish and then shared her idea respectfully.
items.answer: B) She waited for her partner to finish and then shared her idea respectfully.

steps: After the reminder, the student corrected herself — she waited and took her turn appropriately.
This shows she can follow the rule of speaking one at a time after a reminder.

items.prompt:
Which of these responses best 'builds on' what a classmate says?
Classmate: 'I think the frog in the story was brave.'
A) Response: 'I like pizza.'
B) Response: 'I agree — especially when he jumped over the river. That was the bravest part.'
items.answer: B) Response: 'I agree — especially when he jumped over the river. That was the bravest part.'

steps: Option A ignores what the classmate said and introduces an unrelated topic.
Option B agrees and adds a specific, connected detail from the text — this builds on the classmate's idea.

items.prompt:
Two students are discussing what they want to be when they grow up. Student A says, 'I want to be a teacher.' Student B says, 'My teacher is nice.' Is Student B building on the conversation, or slightly off-topic?
A) Building on the conversation — 'teacher' is connected.
B) Slightly off-topic — Student B should ask about why Student A wants to be a teacher.
items.answer: B) Slightly off-topic — Student B should ask about why Student A wants to be a teacher.

steps: Student A shared a personal goal. A stronger response would connect directly: 'Why do you want to be a teacher?' or 'I want to be a doctor.'
Student B's comment about their teacher is loosely related but does not engage with Student A's goal.
For Medium difficulty, we expect students to identify the slightly better response.

items.prompt:
During a book discussion, a student asks: 'Why did the wolf knock on the door?' Is this a good question for a collaborative conversation?
A) No — it is too simple.
B) Yes — it asks for information about the topic under discussion and invites others to share their thinking.

steps: Standard 1.SL.A.1c says students should ask questions to clear up confusion about topics under discussion.
This question is about the book they are discussing — it is relevant and invites participation.

items.prompt:
Which student is following conversation rules BEST in a small group?
A) Luis, who listens carefully to every speaker and waits his turn to contribute.
B) Zoe, who repeats what everyone says without adding any new ideas.

steps: Luis listens and waits his turn — both important rules.
Zoe, while not interrupting, is not contributing new ideas. Building on others means adding new thinking, not just repeating.

items.prompt:
Read this exchange:
Teacher: 'What did we learn about butterflies today?'
Kim: 'They start as caterpillars.'
Pat: 'And they make a chrysalis before they become butterflies!'
Kim: 'Oh! I didn't know that. Does the chrysalis look like a shell?'

What does Kim do in her last comment that shows great conversation skills?
items.answer: Kim asks a question to learn more about what Pat said. She builds the conversation by showing curiosity and asking for additional information.

steps: Kim listens carefully to Pat's new information.
She acknowledges learning something new ('I didn't know that').
She asks a follow-up question to get more details — a strong collaborative conversation move.

items.prompt:
A student keeps talking in a group discussion and never lets anyone else share. Which rule is he breaking?
A) Speaking one at a time
B) Staying on topic
C) Participating equally and letting others speak
items.answer: C) Participating equally and letting others speak

steps: He is technically speaking 'one at a time' (no one else is talking), but he is monopolizing the discussion.
Good conversation requires that all participants have a chance to contribute.
The issue is fairness and balance in participation.

items.prompt:
Which is a better way to disagree in a conversation?
A) 'You're wrong about that.'
B) 'I see it differently — I think the character was scared, not angry, because she was hiding.'
items.answer: B) 'I see it differently — I think the character was scared, not angry, because she was hiding.'

steps: Option A is blunt and could hurt feelings — not respectful.
Option B expresses a different view politely and supports it with evidence from the text.
Respectful disagreement with evidence is a higher-level conversation skill.

items.prompt:
After a read-aloud, the teacher asks, 'What was your favorite part?' Student A says, 'The ending.' Student B says, 'The middle when the dog found the bone — it was funny!' Whose answer better builds on the classroom conversation?
A) Student A
B) Student B

steps: Student A gives a minimal answer with no detail.
Student B names a specific part and explains why — this adds meaning to the discussion and invites others to respond.

items.prompt:
What does 'gaining the floor in a respectful way' mean in a group discussion?
A) Standing on the floor
B) Waiting for a pause and letting others know you have something to add
items.answer: B) Waiting for a pause and letting others know you have something to add

steps: 'Gaining the floor' means getting a turn to speak. Doing it respectfully means not interrupting — waiting for a pause or raising a hand.

items.prompt:
Read the exchange:
Marcus: 'I think the author wanted us to feel happy at the end.'
Lena: 'I felt a little sad, actually. The puppy had to leave its mom.'
Marcus: 'That's true. I guess it was a mix of happy and sad.'

What does Marcus do in his last comment that shows a good conversation skill?
items.answer: Marcus listens to Lena's different perspective, considers it, and updates his thinking to include both views. This shows flexibility and genuine engagement with his partner's idea.

steps: Marcus does not dismiss Lena's point. He acknowledges it ('That's true').
He then revises his own idea ('a mix of happy and sad') based on Lena's input.
Changing your thinking based on a partner's point is a high-level collaboration skill.

items.prompt:
Why is it important to ask questions during a class discussion — not just at the end?
A) It is only polite to ask questions at the end.
B) Asking questions during a discussion keeps the conversation going and helps everyone understand better.
items.answer: B) Asking questions during a discussion keeps the conversation going and helps everyone understand better.

steps: Questions can arise at any point in a discussion.
Asking in the moment allows the speaker to clarify immediately, while the idea is still fresh.
Waiting to the end may mean forgetting the question or losing the chance for clarification.

items.prompt:
A student says she feels too shy to share in group discussions. What is the best advice?
A) Never talk in group discussions.
B) Start small — share one short idea or ask one question each discussion.
items.answer: B) Start small — share one short idea or ask one question each discussion.

steps: Everyone can participate in conversation, even if shy.
Starting with small contributions builds confidence.
Over time, participation grows.

items.prompt:
In a group discussion about a book, which comment is the MOST collaborative?
A) 'I liked the story.'
B) 'I agree with Rosa that the story was exciting. I also thought the ending was surprising because the cat came back.'
items.answer: B) 'I agree with Rosa that the story was exciting. I also thought the ending was surprising because the cat came back.'

steps: Option B names a classmate ('Rosa'), connects to her idea, AND adds a new specific detail.
This is a model of building on others' talk — citing the peer and extending the idea.
